prompt.context: Your client is a premium brand apparel retailer. In recent years it has noticed a consistent decrease in market share.
prompt.question: How would you structure your analysis?

clarifying_info.q: How much has market share fallen?
clarifying_info.a: Market share has fallen from 15% to 7%.
Competitors consist of premium retailers in the same business segment. There is growing competition from substitutes and mid-range brands as well.

clarifying_info.q: Has the overall market size changed?
clarifying_info.a: The market size has been growing steadily.

clarifying_info.q: Have there been any major industry consolidations?
clarifying_info.a: No recent major consolidations in the industry.

clarifying_info.q: Have there been changes in marketing, pricing, or distribution?
clarifying_info.a: No substantial changes in the company's marketing mix or distribution. Prices have remained constant. Competitor marketing, pricing, and product mix has remained unchanged.

clarifying_info.q: What does the distribution network look like?
clarifying_info.a: Distribution is primarily through large retail outlets that stock multiple products (70%). The balance (30%) is distributed through self-owned outlets and smaller merchants.
Distributors have recently launched their own premium product brands.

clarifying_info.q: Is there an online sales channel?
clarifying_info.a: Currently there is no online sales channel.

clarifying_info.q: Have costs or profit margins changed?
clarifying_info.a: No recent changes in cost structure or profit margins.

clarifying_info.q: What is the level of brand recognition?
clarifying_info.a: Customer recognition of the company's brand is low.

framework: Understand market share decline context: overall market growing yet client losing share — isolates issue to relative competitiveness, not market contraction
Examine distribution channel dynamics: 70% through large retail outlets that now carry competing house brands — shelf space and sales push incentive misalignment
Assess marketing and branding: low brand recognition means weak customer pull through distributors; client relies on push model that distributor can undermine
Evaluate current channel mix: only 30% through owned/smaller channels; heavy dependence on hostile distributor creates structural vulnerability
Identify options to diversify distribution: more self-owned stores, online channel, smaller independent merchants
Assess branding investment: build customer pull so consumers demand client products regardless of channel
Consider brand impact of each new channel: premium brand perception must be preserved across any expansion

questions.prompt: What is the root cause of the market share decline?
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies that the market is growing (so the problem is not market contraction) and that prices and competitor behavior are unchanged (so the problem is not pricing or new competition per se). The key insight is that the company's primary distribution channel (large retail outlets, 70% of sales) has launched its own competing premium brands. These distributors control shelf space and earn higher margins on their own products than on the client's products, so they actively push their own brands at the client's expense. With low brand recognition, customers cannot generate pull demand — they buy what is stocked and promoted.

questions.prompt: What strategic options should the client consider to address the decline?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recommend diversifying distribution channels to reduce dependence on hostile distributors. Primary options: (1) expand self-owned stores to capture full margin and control brand presentation; (2) launch an online sales channel to reach customers directly without distributor intermediation. In each case, candidate should note the need to preserve the premium brand image in new channels. Additionally, a significant branding program to build customer recognition and pull demand would support both old and new channels.

brainstorming.prompt: What distribution channel and brand-building options should the client explore?

categories.name: Direct-to-Consumer Channels
ideas: Expand self-owned retail stores in high-traffic premium locations
Partner with premium department stores with dedicated brand zones
Pop-up shops and experiential retail events

categories.name: Indirect Channel Management
ideas: Renegotiate shelf-space agreements with large retail outlets
Offer distributors performance incentives tied to client product sales
Audit and reduce share of sales through hostile distributors
Identify and grow relationships with smaller independent merchants

categories.name: Brand Building
ideas: Invest in brand awareness campaigns to drive customer pull
Develop customer loyalty and recognition programs
Leverage social media and influencer marketing for premium positioning
Improve in-store visual merchandising where still stocked by distributors

recommendation: The client should diversify its distribution channel mix by expanding self-owned stores and launching an online sales channel to reduce reliance on large retail distributors who now compete directly with the client's products

The client should simultaneously invest in a significant branding program to build customer recognition, creating pull demand that forces all channels — existing and new — to carry and promote the client's products
risks: New owned stores and an e-commerce platform require capital investment and operational capability the client may need to build
Expanding owned channels could antagonize remaining cooperative distributors if not managed carefully
Premium brand perception could be diluted if new channels (e.g., online) are not positioned and executed at a consistent quality level
next_steps: Quantify the revenue and margin impact of building owned stores vs. launching online channel
Conduct customer research to understand brand perception gaps and define branding investment required
Develop a channel transition roadmap that phases out dependence on hostile distributors without disrupting total sales volume
